document.title: Motion to Intervene and Protest of the Data Center Coalition to PJM Interconnection, L.L.C.’s proposal to establish Interim Resource Adequacy Service and a Large Load Registry

pages.text:
UNITED STATES OF AMERICA 
BEFORE THE 
FEDERAL ENERGY REGULATORY COMMISSION 
) 
PJM Interconnection, L.L.C. 
 ) 
 Docket No. ER26-3515-000
) 
 
MOTION TO INTERVENE  
AND PROTEST OF THE DATA CENTER COALITION 
 
Pursuant to Rules 211, 212, and 214 of the Rules of Practice and Procedure of the Federal 
Energy Regulatory Commission (“FERC” or the “Commission”)1 and the Commission’s August 
13, 2026 Combined Notice of Filings #2,2 the Data Center Coalition (“DCC”) hereby moves to 
intervene and submits this protest of PJM Interconnection, L.L.C.’s (“PJM”) proposal to establish 
Interim Resource Adequacy Service (“IRAS”) and a Large Load Registry.3 
I. 
INTRODUCTION 
DCC is the membership organization for the U.S. data center industry, representing leading 
data center owners and operators that develop, operate, and maintain data center infrastructure and 
teams across the country.  DCC members operate data centers that constitute significant loads 
within the PJM region and DCC has been an active stakeholder in regional efforts to ensure 
reliability, enable new generation, and discipline load forecasts.   
DCC and its members have been at the forefront of efforts to advance reforms in PJM and 
at the state level to accommodate the growth of data centers and other large load customers within 
the PJM region while maintaining reliability and protecting existing retail customers.  DCC agrees

2 PJM Interconnection, L.L.C., et al., Docket No. ER26-3515-000, et al., Combined Notice of Filings #2 
(Aug. 13, 2026). 
3 PJM Interconnection, L.L.C., Docket No. ER26-3515-000, Proposal of PJM Interconnection, L.L.C. to

with PJM that steps must be taken to maintain reliability, protect existing customers from 
inappropriate cost shifts, and ensure that data centers and other large load customers take 
appropriate responsibility for supporting the development of new generation and infrastructure 
necessary to serve their demand.   
Indeed, DCC was a leading voice in the PJM Critical Issue Fast Path (“CIFP”) processes 
that led to PJM’s Filing in this docket.  From the outset of these processes, DCC championed 
reforms to enable data centers to bring their own generation capacity to insulate existing customers 
from the costs of serving demand from large load customers, as well as legally-durable pathways 
to enable states to implement interruptible retail tariffs to support grid-wide reliability and 
resilience.  Looking beyond the positions DCC took in PJM’s stakeholder process, DCC members 
have proudly joined over 200 governors, utilities, electric cooperatives, and data center developers 
in support of the White House’s “Ratepayer Protection Pledge,”4 which, through historic levels of 
industry investment in long-needed new capacity, is already helping to resolve many of the 
fundamental issues PJM aims to address through this proceeding. 
DCC also strongly supports state efforts to establish interruptible service tariffs that 
facilitate the integration of new large loads while maintaining reliability and protecting existing 
customers.  In fact, DCC has, alongside the Virginia State Corporation Commission (“VA SCC”), 
called for other state regulators to develop model retail interruptible tariffs and emergency load-
reduction programs that would allow large loads to take interruptible service, establish 
standardized curtailment obligations and operating rules, and allow state-jurisdictional utilities to 
curtail participating large commercial and industrial customers during system emergencies to 
 
4 Ratepayer Protection Pledge, THE WHITE HOUSE, Proclamation No. 11014, 91 Fed. Reg. 11439 (Mar. 4, 
2026), https://www.whitehouse.gov/releases/2026/03/ratepayer-protection-pledge/.

- 3 - 
protect existing customers.5   
 
Notwithstanding DCC’s support for bring-your-own-generation-capacity solutions and the 
other initiatives described above, DCC believes that the IRAS proposal is legally defective and 
must be rejected.  The Federal Power Act (“FPA”) grants states—not PJM or FERC—exclusive 
authority over the rates, terms, and conditions of retail service.  Yet, PJM asks the Commission to 
grant it authorization to impose a new curtailment program that aims to interrupt retail service to 
large load customers that PJM determines have failed to comply with new bring your own new 
capacity (“BYONC”) requirements prescribed in the PJM tariff (“Eligible New Large Loads”).  
Rather than accommodating state efforts to modify retail curtailment policies to account for the 
growth of large loads, IRAS instead seeks to compel states within the PJM footprint to conform 
their retail curtailment frameworks to PJM tariff requirements.  DCC believes that this top-down 
approach to addressing the curtailment of retail customers is inconsistent with principles of 
cooperative federalism and disregards the carefully calibrated division of authority between FERC 
and the states.   
 
DCC acknowledges that successfully addressing the challenges of large load integration in 
the region will require collaboration and cooperation among PJM, state regulators, large loads, 
electric distribution companies, and other stakeholders.  But Congress’s decision to reserve to the 
states authority over retail service means that it is the states that must take the lead in developing 
the retail service frameworks through which new large loads are integrated into the electric system, 
including the rules governing the priority of customer classes, the terms for interrupting service to 
retail customers, and the requirements that customers must meet to obtain firm service.  While  
 
5 See Exh. A; Letter to Ms. Paula Conboy and Mr. David Mills from VA SCC Chair, Kelsey Bagot and DCC 
President & CEO, Josh Levi (June 30, 2026), https://www.pjm.com/-/media/DotCom/committees-groups/cifp-
rbp/2026/20260630/20260630-written-comments---va-scc-and-data-center-coalition.pdf.

- 4 - 
PJM has a critical role to play in ensuring that large loads are integrated into the system reliably, 
it should not seek to displace the role of the states by imposing a uniform retail curtailment policy 
across the PJM region. 
 
This does not mean that PJM and the Commission are powerless to take actions to protect 
customers from service interruptions when grid conditions are tight.  During the CIFP process, 
DCC outlined a framework for a state “opt-in framework” that would couple state-led 
implementation of interruptible service with changes to PJM’s operational practices to ensure that 
retail curtailments are implemented in a manner that recognizes the respective roles of wholesale 
and retail regulators.6  Under that proposal, states would be responsible for establishing 
interruptible customer classes for large load customers while PJM would continue to monitor 
system conditions and, when conditions warrant, would issue a signal to utilities in participating 
states that would trigger curtailments in accordance with state-established tariffs and service 
priorities.  To provide immediate relief to customers while states work to update their retail tariffs, 
DCC also proposed that PJM update its manual load-shed procedures to establish a framework 
under which data centers and other large loads would be contacted during emergencies and 
provided an opportunity to voluntarily curtail prior to PJM’s implementation of broader load dump 
procedures.   
DCC’s proposal illustrates that there are approaches that can achieve the same reliability 
outcomes as IRAS while respecting the traditional division of responsibility between FERC and 
the states.  But the benefits of a state-led approach are not limited to merely avoiding the significant

Grid

rbp/2026/20260611/20260611-item-03a---data-center-coalition-presentation.pdf.

- 5 - 
legal issues presented by IRAS.  Allowing states to take the lead in establishing retail curtailment 
priorities avoids one of the other major shortcomings of IRAS: there is no assurance that a PJM-
led framework will be effective or achieve the objectives that PJM seeks.  If states are truly free to 
establish different curtailment priorities as PJM claims, PJM cannot ensure that the customers it 
seeks to target through IRAS will be curtailed, that retail customers that comply with PJM’s 
BYONC requirements will avoid service interruptions, or that the proposal will deliver the 
reliability benefits PJM claims.  
IRAS is also unjust, unreasonable, and unduly discriminatory on its own terms.  IRAS 
would create a sub-class of Network Integration Transmission Service (“NITS”) customers that 
would be defined by the characteristics of the retail customers that they serve.  NITS customers 
serving Eligible New Large Loads would be required to pay the same transmission and capacity 
charges as other NITS customers, but would be curtailed ahead of other NITS customers and firm 
point-to-point customers.  In fact, while NITS customers serving Eligible New Large Loads still 
would be required to pay charges reflecting the cost of capacity committed through PJM’s capacity 
market, PJM proposes to curtail these customers prior to deploying Demand Resources that have 
been committed to provide capacity to maintain reliability and avoid interruptions to firm 
customers.  The result would be to force these NITS customers to bear the costs of capacity that 
would not be available to meet their needs. 
Compounding these problems is the fact that the Filing offers no transition mechanism and 
effectively provides New Large Loads a window of less than ten months to procure new capacity 
or face curtailment—an interval that PJM’s own documented difficulties in bringing resources 
online demonstrates is not realistic.  The result is that large loads that have spent billions of dollars

- 6 - 
and entered complex commercial arrangements in reliance on PJM’s longstanding rules will 
suddenly face the prospect of being unable to obtain the reliable service their projects depend on.   
 
Rather than implementing measures to degrade the quality of service provided to Eligible 
New Large Loads, PJM should be pursuing reforms that eliminate barriers to the development of 
the new generation capacity needed to maintain reliability and avoid the curtailment of retail 
customers.  Yet, PJM proposes to undermine the ability of the capacity market to send price signals 
for the development of new capacity by excluding Eligible New Large Loads from the calculation 
of the Variable Resource Requirement curve (“VRR Curve”) beginning with the 2029/2030 
Delivery Year.  Ultimately, the result will be a capacity market that produces prices and results 
that are untethered to actual supply and demand conditions within the PJM footprint.  A capacity 
market that is modeled as if a large and growing increment of demand does not exist cannot send 
the price signals needed to attract the supply that PJM says the region lacks.  
DCC recognizes that the PJM region must adapt to this high load growth environment in 
which new resource entry remains frustrated and is committed to advancing durable solutions that 
preserve states’ role in integrating large loads, protect existing customers from inappropriate cost 
shifts, and provide data centers and other large loads with timely pathways to power that ultimately 
improves reliability throughout the region.  Establishing a framework that can accomplish these 
objectives is essential to ensuring that America’s industries of the future—data centers, 
semiconductors, battery manufacturing, and the automotive, steel, metal, chemical, petrochemical, 
and refining industries—remain competitive in the global economy.  But PJM’s proposal to impose 
a retail curtailment scheme on states that eviscerates the jurisdictional lines drawn by Congress, 
requires customers to pay for capacity that they will not benefit from, undermines the settled

- 7 - 
expectations of New Large Loads, and may ultimately prove unworkable is not a viable path 
forward.   
For the foregoing reasons, DCC asks the Commission to issue an order rejecting the Filing 
and encouraging PJM to work with stakeholders to develop changes to PJM’s emergency 
procedures that accommodate—rather than dictate—the retail curtailment priorities of individual 
states.  Alternatively, if the Commission finds that the growth of large loads has rendered PJM’s 
existing emergency procedures unjust and unreasonable, the Commission should initiate a Section 
206 proceeding to develop proposed revisions to these procedures that respect the jurisdictional 
boundaries established by the FPA while protecting existing retail customers from service 
disruptions and inappropriate cost shifts.   
If the Commission does not reject IRAS outright, then it should direct PJM to establish a 
meaningful transition mechanism that avoids disrupting existing contractual arrangements and 
provides both large load customers and the states a reasonable timeline to take the steps necessary 
to adapt to the IRAS framework.  Among other things, any transition mechanism should limit the 
application of IRAS in a manner that respects existing contracts and investment decisions, 
including exempting large load customers that have already entered into contracts for retail service 
that pre-date implementation of IRAS.  Additionally, the Commission should direct PJM to delay 
implementation of IRAS until June 1, 2028 to provide new large loads a reasonable amount of 
time to comply with PJM’s BYONC requirements and to provide state authorities with the time 
necessary to update their retail policies to account for the IRAS framework.

- 8 - 
II. 
PROTEST 
A. 
IRAS Unlawfully Intrudes On State Authority Over Retail Sales 
In drafting the FPA, “Congress meant to draw a bright line easily ascertained, between 
state and federal jurisdiction[.]”7  Congress granted FERC jurisdiction over wholesale sales of 
electricity and transmission service in interstate commerce.8  At the same time, the FPA “limits 
FERC’s regulatory reach, and . . . maintains a zone of exclusive state jurisdiction”9 by reserving 
to the states jurisdiction over “any other sale of electric energy” and “over facilities used for the 
generation of electric energy” and “facilities used in local distribution[.]”10   
Although the “wholesale and retail markets in electricity are inextricably linked,” the mere 
fact that the rates, terms, and conditions of retail service may affect wholesale markets is not a 
sufficient basis for FERC to assert jurisdiction.11  FERC cannot take an action transgressing the 
limits prescribed by Congress “no matter how direct, or dramatic, its impact on wholesale rates.”12  
FERC may not approve tariff provisions that directly regulate retail customers, dictate retail 
service terms, or prescribe the curtailment priority of retail customers.13  Nor may FERC approve 
tariff provisions that “target” those matters left for the states to regulate.14  
PJM portrays IRAS as a narrow reliability measure that merely supplements existing 
emergency procedures.  But the proposal cannot be evaluated based on labels alone.  The

8 16 U.S.C. § 824(b)(1).    
9 FERC v. Elec. Power Supply Ass’n, 577 U.S. 260, 266 (2015).  
10 16 U.S.C. § 824(b)(1).  
11 FERC v. Elec. Power Supply Ass’n, 577 U.S. 260, 264 (2015). 
12 Id. at 280. 
13 Northern States Power Co. v. FERC, 176 F.3d 1090 (8th Cir. 1999) (finding that FERC’s “attempt to 
regulate the curtailment of electrical transmission on native/retail consumers is unlawful, as it falls outside of the 
FPA’s specific grant of authority to FERC.”); Tri-State Generation and Transmission Association, Inc., 193 FERC ¶ 
61,070, at P 49 (2025) (rejecting large load tariff that “appear[s] to dictate certain terms and conditions for retail 
sales[.]”). 
14 Oneok, Inc. v. Learjet, Inc., 575 U.S. 373, 385 (2015).

- 9 - 
Commission must examine what IRAS actually does in practice.  When PJM’s Filing and proposed 
tariff language are considered as a whole, the target of the Filing becomes clear: IRAS is an 
unprecedented program that aims to interrupt service to specific retail customers that do not 
comply with federally-approved resource procurement requirements prescribed by the PJM tariff 
and directs state-regulated distribution utilities to implement PJM’s retail curtailment priorities.   
PJM casts IRAS as a new wholesale service that retail customers can provide.  But IRAS 
is not a novel form of demand response; it is a framework for singling out retail customers for 
forced service interruptions during tight grid conditions based on criteria established in a FERC-
jurisdictional tariff.  Under IRAS, “end-use customer load” with a peak load of 50 MW or greater 
that goes into service15 after PJM prescribed deadlines (i.e., New Large Loads) will be required to 
bring capacity meeting PJM’s BYONC criteria or be deemed to be subject to interruption during 
emergency conditions.  In effect, IRAS: 
• seeks to create a new interruptible retail customer class consisting of large load 
customers that do not meet PJM’s BYONC requirements;16 
• authorizes PJM to issue curtailment instructions during prescribed conditions to 
compel Electric Distributors17 to reduce the load of these customers;18  
• directs Electric Distributors to provide compensation to Eligible New Large Loads 
whose load is curtailed pursuant to these directives equal to 50% of the Non-
Performance Charge Rate set out in the PJM tariff (unless the Eligible New Large 
Load agrees to “accept in its retail rates” a lower sum);19 and  
 
15 Filing, Transmittal Letter at 1, n.2 (defining “New Large Load” to include end-use customer load that is 
either “a Large Load that goes into service after” the deadline prescribed by the tariff or “incremental load in-service 
after [such deadline], that increases the existing end-use customer load at a single electrical site that, prior to such 
incremental load, did not previously meet the definition of Large Load.”). 
16 Id. at 69.  
17 Electric Distributor is defined as a PJM member that owns or leases electric distribution facilities that are 
used to provide electric distribution service to load within the PJM region or a cooperative or joint municipal agency 
that has a member that owns electric distribution facilities used to provide electric distribution service to load within 
the PJM region.  PJM, Reliability Assurance Agreement Among Load Serving Entities in the PJM Region, Art. 1 
(defining Electric Distributor).  
18 Filing, Transmittal Letter at 74-75, 83-84. 
19 Id. at 102.

- 10 - 
• directs Electric Distributors to impose charges on other customers to fund these 
compensation payments.20 
PJM has failed to provide a sufficient basis for the Commission to find that IRAS does not 
regulate the terms and conditions of retail service in ways that go beyond the Commission’s 
authority.  FERC does not have any authority to exercise jurisdiction over the quality of service 
that retail customers receive, the terms and conditions that retail customers must meet to avoid 
interruption during emergency conditions, or the compensation paid to retail customers whose 
service is curtailed.  Each of these areas are matters that states have historically regulated pursuant 
to their exclusive authority over the rates, terms, and conditions of retail service.   
The extent to which IRAS targets matters within the jurisdiction of the states is readily 
discernable by even a cursory review of the subject matters addressed by state laws and tariffs 
governing retail service.  For instance, state laws and tariffs within the PJM region recognize the 
authority of state public utility commissions to establish the relative priority of retail customers for 
service,21 require state electric utilities to implement curtailments in a manner that complies with 
state law and regulation, establish interruptible service classes,22 determine eligibility for 
participation in interruptible rate schedules,23 and establish credits and compensation for customers

21 See, e.g., Va. Code § 56-250 (authorizing Virginia state corporation commission to establish plan 
governing curtailment of retail customers during grid emergencies and shortages); 20 VAC5-300-20 (establishing 
procedures for Virginia utilities to take during emergencies and establishing relative priority of residential, 
commercial, and industrial customers);  Ohio Administrative Code 4901:5-19 (recognizing right of Public Utility 
Commission of Ohio to implement measures that fulfill “electric requirements for priority use by its consumers” and 
reallocate or curtail supplies “among its consumers”).  
22 See, e.g., PPL Electric Utilities Corp., General Tariff: Rules and Rate Schedules for Electric Service, Rate

“interruptible service . . . instead of firm service”). 
23 See, e.g., Pub. Util. Comm’n of Ohio, In the Matter of the Application of Ohio Power Company for

tariff for customers that meet notice requirements and establishing demand credits).

- 11 - 
that interrupt their service.24  The service classification of retail customers, the curtailment priority 
of different classes, and the consideration paid for these service interruptions are all familiar 
components of state-regulated retail service and beyond the bounds of permissible FERC 
regulation.  
PJM attempts to justify its proposal by stating that it will not curtail specific end-use 
customers directly, but will direct Electric Distributors25 to curtail these customers’ demand.26  But 
the fact that PJM does not have authority to directly curtail retail customers merely reinforces that 
PJM is attempting to exercise control over matters that are outside of its purview and beyond the 
boundaries of the Commission’s jurisdiction.  And the fact that PJM is attempting to do indirectly 
what it cannot do directly is of no legal significance.27  The FPA leaves no room either for FERC 
to directly regulate retail sales or approve regulations that would indirectly achieve this result. 
PJM argues that IRAS is consistent with the Supreme Court’s determination in EPSA that 
Order No. 745’s directive to regional transmission organizations (“RTO”) and independent system 
operators (“ISO”) to pay demand response resources participating in the energy market the 
locational price for energy did not intrude on the jurisdiction of the states.28  But the reasoning that 
the Court employed in sustaining Order No. 745 in EPSA has no application to IRAS.   
Importantly, EPSA upheld Order No. 745 based on the Court’s determination that Order 
No. 745 merely established a rate for wholesale transactions and was confined solely to the rules

competitive retail suppliers—rather than the Electric Distributor—may be responsible for providing service to retail

26 Filing, Transmittal Letter at 86.

28 FERC v. Elec. Power Supply Ass’n, 577 U.S. 260, 266 (2015).

tariff revisions seek to prescribe the amount paid to retail customers through their retail rates for 
service interruptions implemented at PJM’s direction.30  And, in contrast to Order No. 745, the 
effectiveness of PJM’s proposed framework depends on electric distributors issuing directives to 
their retail customers to reduce demand31 and state regulatory authorities adopting retail tariffs that 
align with the curtailment priorities set forth in the PJM tariff.32  
 
The Court also noted that Order No. 745 was carefully crafted to preserve the jurisdiction 
of the states by providing state regulators with the option of prohibiting retail customers from 
offering demand response into the wholesale markets33 and FERC’s “justifications for regulating 
demand response are all about, and only about, improving the wholesale market.”34  IRAS does 
not provide state regulators with any such opt out.  Regardless of the decisions made by individual 
state regulators, PJM will continue to issue directives to electric distributors to curtail New Large 
Load customers that do not comply with PJM’s BYONC requirements.  And while the 
justifications for Order No. 745 were all about the wholesale market, PJM acknowledges that IRAS 
is intended to “establish load reduction priorities for retail customers”35 and encourage “states to

re-evaluate load reduction plans.”36  The objective of IRAS is clear: to compel state regulators to 
modify their regulation of the retail market to conform to PJM policy.  
Additionally, Order No. 745 established the rate that demand response providers would be 
paid if they voluntarily elected to participate in the wholesale markets.  The wholesale demand 
response programs at issue in Order No. 745 did not compel retail customers to curtail their loads 
involuntarily or state regulators to re-evaluate their retail curtailment programs.  IRAS, in contrast, 
targets individual retail customers that fail to comply with PJM’s BYONC requirements for 
involuntary curtailment and seeks to ensure that states conform their curtailment policies to align 
with the priorities established by the PJM tariff. 
PJM attempts to avoid these jurisdictional issues by claiming that states retain discretion37 
over how to shape their retail policies in response to IRAS and that it will be Electric Distributors 
and state regulators that determine which retail customers actually are curtailed.  PJM’s reasoning 
misses the point.  It is the role of the states—not PJM—to establish load reduction priorities for 
retail service.  Neither PJM nor FERC should be dictating retail curtailment rules, whether directly 
or by establishing market rules intended to compel compliance.  
Ultimately, IRAS does not offer states a genuine choice.  For a state to ignore PJM’s 
dictates would be to run the risk that reliability events could result in broader service disruptions 
affecting other customers within its jurisdiction rather than a more targeted curtailment of 
individual large load customers.  Offering states the choice between compliance and indiscriminate 
curtailment of retail customers is well past the point at which “pressure turns into compulsion” and

undermines the cooperative federalism embodied in the FPA.38 
Even if states were given a meaningful choice, PJM’s repeated references to the discretion 
of the states as to whether to comply with IRAS highlights a fundamental flaw in PJM’s proposal. 
PJM cannot simultaneously maintain that states retain meaningful discretion over the 
implementation of retail curtailments and assume that IRAS will operate exactly as PJM describes.  
If states are genuinely free to establish different curtailment priorities, PJM cannot guarantee that 
the customers it seeks to target through IRAS will actually be curtailed or that the proposal will 
achieve its objectives.  
Nor can PJM ensure that new large load customers that comply with PJM’s BYONC 
requirements will avoid service interruption.  For instance, an Eligible New Large Load customer 
that procures new capacity to meet its load may still experience service disruptions during 
emergency conditions if the relevant state authorities and Electric Distributors do not adopt 
curtailment priorities that align with the IRAS framework.  The lack of certainty that a customer 
that complies with PJM’s BYONC requirements will avoid service interruptions will undermine 
one of the primary justifications for the IRAS framework: to provide an incentive for new large 
load customers to support the development of new capacity required to meet their needs. 
PJM states that IRAS is merely an example of the “federal regime helping to effectuate 
state decisions associated with the rates, terms, and conditions of retail service.”39  But it is quite 
the opposite.  Rather than accommodating state decisions—as the proposal DCC advanced in the 
PJM stakeholder process would have—PJM asks the Commission to approve a tariff framework 
designed to ensure that retail customers are curtailed in a manner that aligns with PJM’s

39 Filing, Transmittal Letter at 3.

- 15 - 
preferences, priorities, and requirements.  If Congress had intended to give FERC the authority to 
determine the retail load priorities within 13 states and the District of Columbia then it would have 
explicitly provided FERC with this authority in the FPA.40  But it did not.  Instead, it explicitly 
denied FERC any authority to exercise jurisdiction over the rates, terms, and conditions of retail 
service, reserving these matters to the states.   
PJM minimizes jurisdictional concerns by noting that the FPA’s drafters could not have 
foreseen the resource adequacy impacts of data centers and technological advancements in 
artificial intelligence.41  That may be true.  But the drafters of the FPA did foresee a different risk: 
that federal regulation of the electric industry could encroach upon the authority long enjoyed by 
the states.  Congress therefore drew a clear jurisdictional boundary, granting FERC authority over 
wholesale sales and interstate transmission while reserving regulation of retail service to the states.  
Implicit in this structure is the recognition that not all problems require a federal solution.  The 
novelty of today’s reliability challenges does not permit the Commission to disregard the 
boundaries established by Congress.

B. 
IRAS Is Unjust, Unreasonable, Unduly Discriminatory, And Inconsistent 
With Cost Causation Requirements 
 
1. 
Curtailing New Large Loads Before Requiring Demand Resources To 
Perform Is Unjust And Unreasonable 
The purpose of committing capacity through the PJM Reliability Pricing Model (“RPM”) 
is to ensure that PJM has sufficient resources available to avoid the risk of supply interruptions.42  
In the last two PJM Base Residual Auctions (“BRA”), Demand Resources were paid over a 
combined $1.5 billion to reduce their demand when called upon by PJM to maintain reliability.43  
Demand Resources are compensated at this level based on “the expectation that such resources 
will be available to provide energy and reserves when called upon” just like other Capacity 
Resources.44   
If IRAS is approved, however, Demand Resources committed through the capacity market 
will no longer be available to serve the needs of Eligible New Large Load customers.  Specifically,

The Data Center Coalition supports PJM’s objective of ensuring that new large loads 
contribute to maintaining system reliability and that sufficient capacity is developed to 
support continued economic growth. We agree that reliability must be maintained and that 
new capacity should accompany significant new load additions. At the same time, 
implementation frameworks must provide clear customer treatment, align obligations with 
benefits, and protect existing customers. 
DCC’s proposal is founded on the principle that large-load integration requires 
coordination among PJM, states, electric distribution companies (EDCs), and customers. 
Durable solutions must recognize the respective roles of wholesale and retail regulators 
while providing certainty regarding reliability obligations, customer protections, and 
curtailment treatment. 
State Opt-In Framework 
DCC proposes a State Opt-In model that allows states and EDCs to establish interruptible 
service classifications and customer treatment rules while PJM continues to administer 
wholesale reliability requirements. Under this approach: 
• States establish interruptible customer classes and associated tariff provisions for large-
load customers. 
• PJM monitors system conditions and, when reliability conditions warrant, issues a 
wholesale reliability signal for interruption of interruptible load. 
• The PJM signal activates the applicable state interruptible tariff. 
• The EDC implements curtailments in accordance with state-established customer 
classifications, priorities, and protections. 
• PJM maintains responsibility for bulk-system reliability, while states retain authority over 
retail customer classifications and curtailment treatment. 
• This approach achieves the desired reliability outcome while preserving the traditional 
division of state and federal responsibilities and avoiding the jurisdictional concerns 
associated with PJM directly imposing mandatory curtailment obligations on retail 
customers.

• The framework also preserves incentives for customers to support the development of 
new capacity resources. 
The proposal acknowledges a practical reality: regardless of the wholesale framework 
adopted, states and EDCs ultimately determine how customers are treated during 
emergency conditions. By explicitly incorporating state implementation into the 
framework, the proposal creates a more transparent and durable path for integrating large-
load growth while maintaining reliability. 
The state-led approach is also necessary to avoid significant jurisdictional concerns. Any 
framework that requires PJM to impose mandatory curtailment obligations based on the 
characteristics of specific retail customers risks blurring the longstanding division between 
wholesale and retail regulation. By relying on states and EDCs to establish customer 
classifications, interruptible service arrangements, and curtailment priorities, the proposal 
preserves the traditional regulatory compact while allowing PJM to maintain reliability 
through wholesale market signals. 
 
Immediate Reliability Action to Protect Residential Customers 
While states develop long-term large-load tariffs and customer classifications, PJM, states, 
and EDCs should take immediate action to strengthen emergency load-shed procedures 
and better protect residential customers. 
DCC proposes a phased manual load-shed approach under which large commercial and 
industrial customers are contacted and provided an opportunity to curtail load before 
residential customers are interrupted during emergency reliability events. States and zones 
without significant large-load customers available for curtailment would not be expected 
to participate in the initial phase. Instead, the first phase would focus on areas where large 
commercial and industrial load reductions can be achieved. Residential customers and 
critical services would remain a last-resort option after practical large-customer 
curtailment opportunities within the affected area have been exhausted. 
This recommendation is significant because it can be implemented immediately and does 
not require states to first complete lengthy tariff, rulemaking, or customer-classification 
proceedings. It provides a practical bridge between today’s reliability challenges and the 
longer-term frameworks currently under development across the PJM region. 
The approach offers several benefits: 
• Provides immediate protection for residential customers. 
• Reduces the likelihood that residential and critical-service customers are interrupted.

• Preserves state authority over retail customer classifications and curtailment priorities. 
• Improves reliability outcomes during emergency conditions using existing operational 
tools and processes. 
• Creates time for states, EDCs, customers, and PJM to develop durable long-term 
solutions without delaying meaningful residential customer protections. 
Conclusion 
DCC’s proposal advances PJM’s reliability objectives while providing a practical 
implementation pathway that aligns responsibilities among PJM, states, EDCs, and 
customers. The State Opt-In framework recognizes the realities of retail implementation, 
preserves incentives for new capacity development, and provides greater clarity regarding 
customer obligations and protections. Combined with immediate actions to better protect 
residential customers during reliability emergencies, the proposal offers both a near-term 
and long-term path for maintaining reliability while supporting continued economic growth 
throughout the PJM region.
